questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t})\cdot 1+(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2{t}^{2}+2$ and $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)\,j \\  & =4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\cdot 4t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\cdot \frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1}{({1}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1} \\  & =\frac{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1)}{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x\,i+2y\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={e}^{-t}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{-t}\,i+2{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =(-{e}^{-t})\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{-t}\,i+2{e}^{t}\,j)\cdot ((-{e}^{-t})\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{-t}\cdot (-{e}^{-t})+2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2{e}^{2(1)}-2{e}^{-2(1)} \\  & =2{e}^{2}-2{e}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Rate of Change of a Multivariable Function at a Point Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t},3t-1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t,y=\sqrt{t}$ and $z=3t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\sqrt{t}(3t-1),2t(3t-1),2t\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩ \\  & =(3t-1)\sqrt{t}\cdot 2+(6{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+2t\sqrt{t}\cdot 3 \\  & =6t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}+6t\sqrt{t} \\  & =12t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =12(1)\sqrt{1}-2\sqrt{1}+\frac{3(1)^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\,i+(2xy+{z}^{3})\,j+3y{z}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{3},y=1,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\,i+3{t}^{3}\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+(0)\,j+\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\,i+3{t}^{3}\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (3{t}^{2}i+(0)\,j+\,k) \\  & =1\cdot 3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}\cdot 0+3{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2} \\  & =6{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
